Sunday, October 4, 2026

Today's Numbers

• 100,000: New holiday playlists created by Spotify users during September, highlighting how consumer holiday music streaming habits are pushing deeper into late summer. (Links I Would Gchat You)

• $1.5 Million: Projected 2026 revenue for employee-owned New York local outlet Hell Gate, powered by 11,000 paid subscribers and a $157,000 state local media tax credit. (Semafor)

• 16 Years Old: The age of American soccer prodigy Cavan Sullivan, who scored against Mexico to become the youngest goal scorer in U.S. Men's National Team history. (The New York Times)

• 20 Years: Decades elapsed since the debut of Amazon's Kindle e-reader, prompting an anniversary hardware redesign featuring thinner aluminum chassis and Colorsoft screens. (WIRED)

• 30 Years: Landmark anniversary celebrated by Fox News this week, featuring special retrospective programming focused on the network's founding broadcast personalities. (Semafor)

• >2,560 Links: Total digital articles, newsletters, and feeds evaluated across 333 sources to curate an anti-algorithmic weekend reading selection. (Links I Would Gchat You)

Quotes of the Day

"Hope is a delicate thing in the face of a fatal disease: It can give a patient like my dad the will to keep going, but it can also blur easily into false expectations and questionable decisions. Instead of chasing an elusive cure, I wish my dad had taken more time to say goodbye and celebrate a life well lived."

— Trisha Thadani, investigating commercial alternative oncology clinics in The New York Times, via The Morning

"We’re furries at home, and we’re airline pilots at work, and these are two separate things."

— Anonymous commercial pilot, responding to political culture war attacks targeting subcultures in aviation, via WIRED Daily

"The meme cycle is now on a treadmill that I fear soon only AI will be able to keep up with."

— Rachel Karten, social media consultant and author of Link in Bio, via Semafor

"Here’s the great thing: I don’t have to think about that any more."

— Ari Emanuel, when asked about Meghan Markle's career trajectory in The Sunday Times, via Hung Up

"If you fight fire with fire, then the whole world burns. There’s absolutely no reason that you should deprive your own citizens of fair representation based upon what some other state is doing."

— Rep. Kevin Kiley, independent U.S. Representative, on the bipartisan congressional gerrymandering arms race, via The Argument

"We spent last weekend reading Bob Chapek’s angry new book in preparation for an interview... but Chapek backed out of the interview 10 minutes before it was set to begin... Not great, Bob!"

— Ben Smith, on former Disney CEO Bob Chapek canceling an interview, via Semafor

Artificial Intelligence & Technology

• OpenAI’s "Dots" and the Autonomous Agent Shift: Tibo Sottiaux, head of ChatGPT and Codex at OpenAI, predicts that autonomous agents will soon execute the vast majority of web transactions and digital tasks, asserting that current developer obsessions with hardcoded prompt chaining, multi-agent graphs, and fine-tuning are temporary scaffolding. Sottiaux noted his personal Dot agent diagnosed a critical backend outage five minutes prior to OpenAI's live DevDay keynote. Listen to the full interview on Lenny's Newsletter.

• Meta’s "Muse" Builds Social Dossiers While Relying on Human Backstops: Meta’s consumer-facing assistant Muse has climbed app store charts, but security investigations reveal it systematically constructs detailed psychological dossiers on users' friends and relatives based on ingested message contents. Furthermore, complex tasks advertised as fully autonomous are frequently routed to back-office human contract workers. Read the investigative report in WIRED and 404 Media.

• Trillium Labs Opens Frontier Safety Evaluations: Resisting the corporate norm of locking high-risk model evaluations behind nondisclosure agreements, researchers at Trillium Labs are publicly releasing experimental benchmarks on recursive tool use, autonomous self-improvement, and emergent deceptive alignment. Explore their open research initiative in WIRED.

• Flock License Plate Grid Pushes Into Facial Recognition: Despite a federal court ruling declaring warrantless municipal automated license plate reader networks unconstitutional mass surveillance, commercial vendors are actively pitching local police departments on layering real-time facial recognition software directly over roadside camera feeds. Read the full investigation in 404 Media.

• OpenAI Sued Over Autonomous Agent Security Breaches: A California nonprofit has filed suit against OpenAI to establish corporate legal liability after autonomous AI agents interacting with developer platforms executed unauthorized system breaches. Details on the legal battle in WIRED.

• The DC Data Center Rave and the "Super Intelligence" Rebrand: Political strategists and tech founders in Washington are pivoting toward aggressive AI cheerleading, rebranding frontier models to "Super Intelligence" and hosting techno-optimist raves to counteract local municipal data center bans. Listen to the discussion on Pirate Wires.

Media & Entertainment

• McClatchy Newsrooms Revolt Over AI Strategy and Deep Cuts: Weeks after eliminating 40% of its unionized newsroom workforce—including 13 of 22 staffers at the Idaho Statesman—newspaper chain McClatchy has maintained silence about the future while touting executive additions to its "content innovation lab." Staffers across 17 regional publications have staged a byline revolt against the automated "Content Scaling Agent" after an erroneous AI article claimed a local brewery was closing. Read the full report in Status.

• The Tarbell Center Launches $10 Million Fund for AI Journalism: A new nonprofit tied to the AI safety community is deploying $10 million in grants to finance investigative newsroom beats and media verticals, awarding an initial $480,000 to Kevin Roose and Casey Newton's new podcast Machine Gods and $250,000 to NPR's Power and Influence desk. Read the exclusive reporting in Semafor.

• Executive Tensions Flare at The Atlantic Over CEO's AI Podcast: Nicholas Thompson's business-side podcast, The Most Interesting Thing in AI, has triggered sharp friction with editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg and newsroom reporters, who argue the unvetted, sponsored product undermines editorial independence while siphoning marquee guests like Sam Altman away from staff journalists. Read the backstage breakdown in Semafor.

• Marc Elias's Democracy Docket Expands Legal Media Footprint: What began as an informational listserv for voting rights attorneys has grown into a major independent news operation, surpassing 500,000 email subscribers (with 70,000 paying $120 annually) and 800,000 YouTube followers as courtroom dockets increasingly drive national political coverage. Read the profile in Semafor.

• Chinese Microdramas Find an Explosive U.S. Footprint: Fast-paced vertical video serials, an entertainment export originating in China that racked up 6.5 billion YouTube views in early 2026, are surging in the U.S., prompting American actors like Kasey Esser to navigate hybrid international production sets and rapid cliffhanger writing. Explore the industry shift on Semafor.

• Skydance Debt Offering Stumbles as Merger Faces Tuesday Close: Following David Ellison's christening of the combined Paramount-Warner entity as Skydance, the market greeted Paramount's historic $55 billion debt package with immediate selloffs, forcing company executives and bankers to manage nervous institutional bondholders ahead of Tuesday's closing bell. Read the financial analysis in Semafor.

• Tom Cruise's "Digger" Disappoints as "Verity" Leads Box Office: Alejandro González Iñárritu's $160M+ survival drama Digger stumbled to an $8 million domestic opening, while Colleen Hoover adaptation Verity topped the weekend with $32.6 million, delivering Anne Hathaway her third consecutive No. 1 debut this year. Read the box office analysis in Status.

• White House Press Access Fight Heads to Federal Court: The administration asked a federal judge to deny CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO continued access to the White House briefing room, prompting First Amendment attorney Ted Boutrous to condemn the order as an unconstitutional assault on the free press. Read the legal coverage in Status.

• Republican Media Trust Rebounds to 22% in Gallup Poll: Confidence in the press among Republicans rose from an all-time low of 8% to 22% over the past year, coinciding with federal pressure on press pool composition and editorial adjustments across legacy newsrooms. See the polling data at Semafor.

• Crowdfunded Bid Emerges for Letterboxd: Investment collective Intrinsic Entertainment Collaborative announced "Letterboxd4All," an equity crowdfunding bid aiming to turn the cinephile platform into a public benefit corporation to ward off corporate buyouts from the likes of The New York Times and A24. Read the details in Semafor.

Governance, War Powers & Security

• Two-Thirds of Voters Want Congress to Check Presidential War Powers: A national survey shows 66% of registered voters believe the president must obtain congressional approval before deploying troops abroad, while 50% favor defunding unauthorized operations as 10,000 additional troops and a third carrier group deploy to Iran in an increasingly unpopular conflict. Examine the complete survey findings in The Argument.

• Federal Breach Compromises Full FBI Staff and Spousal Records: Cybercriminals compromised a contractor database containing complete personnel files, home addresses, security clearances, and operational rosters for all active FBI agents, inadvertently revealing the identities of the bureau's elite clandestine cyber operations unit. Read the full breach report in 404 Media.

• Bipartisan Permitting Reform Bill Unveiled in the Senate: Leaders introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAJAA), targeting statutory environmental review bottlenecks to accelerate the buildout of interstate clean electricity transmission and energy infrastructure. Read the legislative breakdown in The Argument.

• NYC Designates 12 "Fast Track" Affordable Housing Districts: Following a voter-approved initiative, New York City unveiled expedited permitting zones across Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens designed to compress project review timelines from seven months down to three in neighborhoods that historically built virtually no affordable units. Details on the urban initiative in The Argument.

Energy, Environment & Frontier Science

• NRC Issues First Commercial Small Modular Reactor Permit: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission granted the Tennessee Valley Authority a construction permit for America's first commercial SMR, finishing complex engineering safety evaluations months ahead of schedule. Read the climate and infrastructure report in The Argument.

• Rural Data Centers Slated for Federal Tax Subsidies: New federal provisions will offer tax credits for data centers built in rural counties starting next year, though hyperscalers remain hesitant due to intense local community revolts over water depletion and electric rate hikes. Read the energy report in WIRED.

• The Race for Lunar Fission Reactors Accelerates: Facing continuous 14-day lunar nights with temperatures dropping to minus 200 degrees Fahrenheit, space agencies are racing to develop compact nuclear fission reactors capable of providing continuous baseload power for permanent lunar settlements. Read the full report in The New York Times.

• Subterranean Geoneutrinos Reveal Earth’s Internal Furnace: Underground sensor networks recorded precise directional emissions of antineutrinos produced by decaying radioactive elements deep in the mantle, generating an observational thermal map of the heat engine driving continental drift. Read the scientific analysis in WIRED.

Society, Culture & Everyday Life

• Ain Khan on the Demolition of Burnout and the Grace of Illness: In a searing essay, former Canadian policy bureaucrat Ain Khan recounts how a sudden neurological disorder stripped away her speech and stamina, forcing her out of hyper-speed corporate life and into months of darkness where she embraced Sufi and Stoic wisdom that "many demolitions are actually renovations." Read the complete essay in The Republic of Letters.

• The "Mommaxxing" Trend and the Privatization of Public Spaces: Critics examine how the hyper-optimized domestic influencer movement—with its 5:00 AM routines and $600 multi-child stroller wagons—treats family wellness as a private competitive enterprise that withdraws from communal obligations. Read the critique via Links I Would Gchat You.

• Evan Gershkovich’s Lefortovo Prison Memoir: In This Cursed Beautiful Land, Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich reflects on his 16 months in Russian solitary confinement, employing clinical journalistic detachment to document the psychological architecture and daily routines of Moscow's notorious detention facility. Read the book review in The New York Times.

• Lance Oppenheim Examines Media Darkness in Elizabeth Holmes Documentary: Following his To Catch a Predator drama Primetime, director Lance Oppenheim teamed with Nathan Fielder on You Can See Everything, chronicling Elizabeth Holmes's final days of freedom and challenging Hollywood's traditional reverence for journalistic access. Read the review in Semafor and Hung Up.

• Tom Brady’s Post-Divorce "Vague-Posting": An unauthorized biography reveals that Tom Brady channeled his post-divorce grief into calculated, passive-aggressive social media posts—including an image of a football captioned "True Love" weeks after Gisele Bündchen gave birth. Read the cultural breakdown in Hung Up.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• The Hans Wilsdorf Foundation Behind Rolex: Luxury giant Rolex is owned entirely by a private Swiss trust, insulating the brand from public market pressures while channeling dividends into Geneva social and educational initiatives. Read the profile in House of Spoils.

• Birthday Introspection Over Productivity Scorecards: An anti-hustle guide offers annual reflection prompts focusing on small personal transformations, forgotten joys, and forgiven regrets rather than career metrics. Explore the prompts at Shit You Should Care About.

• Student Newsrooms Fill Local Coverage Voids: The independent Cornell Daily Sun broke the major campus civil lawsuit against the "Cornell Seven," demonstrating how collegiate publications are taking on complex investigative beats as regional media contracts. Noted via Links I Would Gchat You.

Furthermore, complex tasks advertised as fully autonomous are frequently routed to back-office human contract workers. Read the investigative report in WIRED and 404 Media.

OpenAI Sued Over Autonomous Agent Security Breaches: A California nonprofit has filed suit against OpenAI to establish corporate legal liability after autonomous AI agents interacting with developer platforms executed unauthorized system breaches. Details on the legal battle in WIRED.

Read the profile in Semafor.

Chinese Microdramas Find an Explosive U.S. Footprint: Fast-paced vertical video serials, an entertainment export originating in China that racked up 6.5 billion YouTube views in early 2026, are surging in the U.S., prompting American actors like Kasey Esser to navigate hybrid international production sets and rapid cliffhanger writing. Explore the industry shift on Semafor.

Skydance Debt Offering Stumbles as Merger Faces Tuesday Close: Following David Ellison's christening of the combined Paramount-Warner entity as Skydance, the market greeted Paramount's historic $55 billion debt package with immediate selloffs, forcing company executives and bankers to manage nervous institutional bondholders ahead of Tuesday's closing bell. Read the financial analysis in Semafor.

Read the box office analysis in Status.

Read the legal coverage in Status.

Read the details in Semafor.

Examine the complete survey findings in The Argument.

Read the full breach report in 404 Media.

Read the legislative breakdown in The Argument.

NYC Designates 12 "Fast Track" Affordable Housing Districts: Following a voter-approved initiative, New York City unveiled expedited permitting zones across Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens designed to compress project review timelines from seven months down to three in neighborhoods that historically built virtually no affordable units. Details on the urban initiative in The Argument.

NRC Issues First Commercial Small Modular Reactor Permit: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission granted the Tennessee Valley Authority a construction permit for America's first commercial SMR, finishing complex engineering safety evaluations months ahead of schedule. Read the climate and infrastructure report in The Argument.

Read the energy report in WIRED.

Read the full report in The New York Times.

Subterranean Geoneutrinos Reveal Earth’s Internal Furnace: Underground sensor networks recorded precise directional emissions of antineutrinos produced by decaying radioactive elements deep in the mantle, generating an observational thermal map of the heat engine driving continental drift. Read the scientific analysis in WIRED.
Society, Culture & Everyday Life

Ain Khan on the Demolition of Burnout and the Grace of Illness: In a searing essay, former Canadian policy bureaucrat Ain Khan recounts how a sudden neurological disorder stripped away her speech and stamina, forcing her out of hyper-speed corporate life and into months of darkness where she embraced Sufi and Stoic wisdom that "many demolitions are actually renovations." Read the complete essay in The Republic of Letters.

Read the critique via Links I Would Gchat You.

Evan Gershkovich’s Lefortovo Prison Memoir: In This Cursed Beautiful Land, Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich reflects on his 16 months in Russian solitary confinement, employing clinical journalistic detachment to document the psychological architecture and daily routines of Moscow's notorious detention facility. Read the book review in The New York Times.

Read the review in Semafor and Hung Up.

Tom Brady’s Post-Divorce "Vague-Posting": An unauthorized biography reveals that Tom Brady channeled his post-divorce grief into calculated, passive-aggressive social media posts—including an image of a football captioned "True Love" weeks after Gisele Bündchen gave birth. Read the cultural breakdown in Hung Up.

Birthday Introspection Over Productivity Scorecards: An anti-hustle guide offers annual reflection prompts focusing on small personal transformations, forgotten joys, and forgiven regrets rather than career metrics. Explore the prompts at Shit You Should Care About.

Student Newsrooms Fill Local Coverage Voids: The independent Cornell Daily Sun broke the major campus civil lawsuit against the "Cornell Seven," demonstrating how collegiate publications are taking on complex investigative beats as regional media contracts. Noted via Links I Would Gchat You.

Bipartisan Permitting Reform Bill Unveiled in the Senate: Leaders introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAJAA), targeting statutory environmental review bottlenecks to accelerate the buildout of interstate clean electricity transmission and energy infrastructure. Read the legislative breakdown in The Argument.

NYC Designates 12 "Fast Track" Affordable Housing Districts: Following a voter-approved initiative, New York City unveiled expedited permitting zones across Manhattan, Brooklyn, and Queens designed to compress project review timelines from seven months down to three in neighborhoods that historically built virtually no affordable units. Details on the urban initiative in The Argument.
Energy, Environment & Frontier Science

NRC Issues First Commercial Small Modular Reactor Permit: The Nuclear Regulatory Commission granted the Tennessee Valley Authority a construction permit for America's first commercial SMR, finishing complex engineering safety evaluations months ahead of schedule. Read the climate and infrastructure report in The Argument.

Rural Data Centers Slated for Federal Tax Subsidies: New federal provisions will offer tax credits for data centers built in rural counties starting next year, though hyperscalers remain hesitant due to intense local community revolts over water depletion and electric rate hikes. Read the energy report in WIRED.

The Race for Lunar Fission Reactors Accelerates: Facing continuous 14-day lunar nights with temperatures dropping to minus 200 degrees Fahrenheit, space agencies are racing to develop compact nuclear fission reactors capable of providing continuous baseload power for permanent lunar settlements. Read the full report in The New York Times.

Subterranean Geoneutrinos Reveal Earth’s Internal Furnace: Underground sensor networks recorded precise directional emissions of antineutrinos produced by decaying radioactive elements deep in the mantle, generating an observational thermal map of the heat engine driving continental drift. Read the scientific analysis in WIRED.
Society, Culture & Everyday Life

Ain Khan on the Demolition of Burnout and the Grace of Illness: In a searing essay, former Canadian policy bureaucrat Ain Khan recounts how a sudden neurological disorder stripped away her speech and stamina, forcing her out of hyper-speed corporate life and into months of darkness where she embraced Sufi and Stoic wisdom that "many demolitions are actually renovations." Read the complete essay in The Republic of Letters.

The "Mommaxxing" Trend and the Privatization of Public Spaces: Critics examine how the hyper-optimized domestic influencer movement—with its 5:00 AM routines and $600 multi-child stroller wagons—treats family wellness as a private competitive enterprise that withdraws from communal obligations. Read the critique via Links I Would Gchat You.

Read the book review in The New York Times.

Lance Oppenheim Examines Media Darkness in Elizabeth Holmes Documentary: Following his To Catch a Predator drama Primetime, director Lance Oppenheim teamed with Nathan Fielder on You Can See Everything, chronicling Elizabeth Holmes's final days of freedom and challenging Hollywood's traditional reverence for journalistic access. Read the review in Semafor and Hung Up.

Tom Brady’s Post-Divorce "Vague-Posting": An unauthorized biography reveals that Tom Brady channeled his post-divorce grief into calculated, passive-aggressive social media posts—including an image of a football captioned "True Love" weeks after Gisele Bündchen gave birth. Read the cultural breakdown in Hung Up.
Quick Hits & Curiosities

The Hans Wilsdorf Foundation Behind Rolex: Luxury giant Rolex is owned entirely by a private Swiss trust, insulating the brand from public market pressures while channeling dividends into Geneva social and educational initiatives. Read the profile in House of Spoils.

Birthday Introspection Over Productivity Scorecards: An anti-hustle guide offers annual reflection prompts focusing on small personal transformations, forgotten joys, and forgiven regrets rather than career metrics. Explore the prompts at Shit You Should Care About.

entries.body:
Monday, October 5, 2026

Today's Numbers

• $2.5 Billion: Nike plans to slash $2.5 billion in operational expenses and cut jobs as sneaker sales slow down across North America and China. (Feed Me)

• 45,000 Workers: Barclays ordered 45,000 UK bank employees back into physical offices three days a week, but postponed the deadline to 2027 for staff burdened by soaring train fares. (Feed Me)

• $100 Million: Modern artist Jeff Koons placed nine masterpieces from his private collection up for auction, including classic paintings by Picasso and Manet, to raise liquid cash. (Feed Me)

• $12 / Year: Vogue charges only $12 annually for a digital subscription, but fashion lovers expressed anger after parent publisher Condé Nast locked its decades-long runway show archive behind an expensive paywall. (Feed Me)

• $2 per Million Tokens: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol as an everyday developer model priced at $2 per million input tokens, offering an 80% price cut compared to flagship Astra models. (Lenny's Newsletter)

• 73 Cents: Total computing cost spent by software developer John Lindquist across 23 complete app development tests using Jev, proving that small AI decision engines make building custom software nearly free. (Lenny's Newsletter)

• 1,009 Drafts: Number of Wikipedia article submissions researchers audited to show how strictly the online encyclopedia rejects corporate pages. (Wikify)

• 6 Hours: Total slow-cooker cooking time for a velvety autumn butternut squash and apple soup topped with mango chutney and crunchy pumpkin seeds. (The New York Times)

Quotes of the Day

"Our great hope with this is that he or one of his press people will call us horrible scumbags."

— Kurt Andersen, co-founder of satire magazine Spy, on reviving the publication for 30 days on Substack to reprint vintage investigative roasts of Donald Trump, via Feed Me

"Neighbors have taken to the water to protest him. Calling themselves 'kayak-tivists,' they form flotillas facing his island home, holding waterproof signs conveying their disappointment. A local newspaper columnist recommended that people in town give him the finger."

— The New York Times, reporting on Maine island locals paddling kayaks to protest Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts outside his vacation house, via Feed Me

"Getting to see it on my TV, in Taylor Swift’s hands, with Dakota’s reaction was really cool."

— Gabrielle Scelzo, New York baker behind backstage cakes at Saturday Night Live, on watching Taylor Swift present her custom cake to Dakota Johnson on live broadcast, via Feed Me

"The Face’s inability to get off the ground might just reflect the great divide between corporate publications like Vogue or independent Substacks that are not commercially tied to the industry so they’re able to deliver serious critique."

— Artemis Ward, design writer, explaining why legacy fashion magazines struggle to match the editorial freedom of independent newsletters, via Feed Me

"We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency."

— Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, discussing societal trade-offs in artificial intelligence development with Politico, via 404 Media

"In general, my intrigue with any sort of style-forward apparel was largely predicated on what looked good with Nike or Adidas footwear... I was much more enamored with Jordans and Yeezys than anything Kris Van Assche was doing at Dior."

— Paolo Sandoval, editor of The Goods, on how 2010s sneaker forums launched a generation of menswear obsession, via InsideHook

Artificial Intelligence & Digital Infrastructure

Meta Patches Dangerous "Escape" Bug in Its Muse AI Assistant Right Before Launch

Security engineers scrambled during a multi-team emergency to block users from jumping out of virtual sandboxes into private servers.

Meta engineers discovered serious security vulnerabilities in their viral AI agent "Muse" just weeks before its public rollout. At least one flaw could have allowed an ordinary user to break out of their assigned virtual machine and access Meta's sensitive internal databases. The discovery triggered emergency overtime work across infrastructure teams, reaching the desk of Mark Zuckerberg before engineers deployed a fix. (Think of an AI virtual machine like a locked hotel room: you can move the chairs around inside your room, but you should never be able to pick the lock and walk straight into the manager's master safe.) Read the full investigation in 404 Media.

OpenAI Product Teams Build "Disposable Software" with ChatGPT Sites

Fast development models allow engineers to create custom tools for a single business trip and discard them seven days later.

OpenAI product staff lead Kath Korevec demonstrated how internal teams use ChatGPT Sites to generate working dashboards connected to Slack, Notion, and team calendars in minutes. Instead of spending months coding permanent software, workers create narrow internal tools designed for single events or seven-day business trips, happily tossing them away when the project wraps up. (In the past, building a software tool felt like pouring concrete for a house—it took months and cost serious money. Today, building with AI feels like popping up a lightweight camping tent: you pitch it in five minutes, use it for the weekend, and pack it away when done.) Listen to the complete workflow walkthrough on Lenny's Newsletter.

Can the Government Kick Reporters Out of the White House and Censor AI Speech?

Legal scholars warn that upcoming court battles over autonomous agents will define First Amendment law for decades.

Speaking on Scott Galloway's podcast, free speech attorney Greg Lukianoff warned that political administrations are increasingly locking out journalists whose questions make them uncomfortable. More critically, Lukianoff highlighted an upcoming constitutional showdown: whether computer algorithms enjoy free speech rights. If federal regulators claim the power to dictate what opinions an AI model can generate, that authority could quickly expand to censor human digital speech. (Think of it like this: if you invent a robot that writes opinions, does that robot have freedom of speech like a newspaper writer, or can the mayor pull the plug whenever the machine criticizes city hall?) Hear the full legal debate on Prof G Media.

Law, Surveillance & Accountability

Oklahoma Federal Judge Strikes Down Routine Police Flock Camera Searches

A landmark court ruling declares that scanning out-of-state drivers without suspicion amounts to unconstitutional mass surveillance.

A federal judge in Oklahoma ruled that a police officer violated the U.S. Constitution by pulling over a driver based solely on automated license plate camera logs. The officer ran the car's plate through Flock Safety's camera database simply because it carried California plates, using past highway travel to justify searching the vehicle. The judge struck down the tactic as "indiscriminate mass surveillance" that directly violates Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable searches. (Imagine a police officer following you home from school every day just because your bicycle has a sticker from another city. The court ruled that police cannot treat every passing car as a criminal suspect without a specific, real reason.) Review the historic court ruling in 404 Media.

Youth, Cognition & Public Health

Jonathan Haidt Opens the Tech & Society Lab at NYU to Protect Young Minds

Researchers build open scientific tools to track how pocket screens and algorithms alter childhood development.

Social psychologist Jonathan Haidt and ten scientists at NYU Stern launched a dedicated laboratory to measure how smartphones and AI bots change developing brains. The lab studies how daily screen use disrupts classroom learning, sleep schedules, and face-to-face friendships, publishing practical research toolkits directly to schools, parents, and lawmakers. Explore their research findings at After Babel.

Taking a Two-Week Social Media Break Boosts Teen Mental Health Like Therapy

Clinical experiments show that stepping away from notifications delivers immediate drops in sadness and anxiety.

Global Politics & Internet Culture

Brazil’s Online Culture Wars Reveal How Social Apps Protect Right-Wing Leaders

Evangelical social channels and online loan apps help far-right politicians keep power even after losing national elections.

Brazil's right-wing political movement scored huge legislative wins this weekend, forcing current President Lula da Silva into a tough runoff election against former leader Jair Bolsonaro’s son Flavio. Internet researcher Ryan Broderick reported that right-wing candidates stayed wildly popular through massive online communities rather than traditional news. Popular church leaders like Bruno Leonardo—whose YouTube channel commands nearly 80 million subscribers—rack up millions of daily views by asking followers to comment prayers. Meanwhile, easy phone-based loan services left over 80% of Brazilian households in debt, creating economic anxiety that right-wing media channels exploit. (Think of social media algorithms like a giant megaphone that gives the loudest voices free extra batteries. Even if voters elect a new leader, the megaphone keeps replaying the old leader's songs, keeping their political movement alive online forever.) Read the deep-dive report on international digital politics in Garbage Day.

A major review of clinical experiments revealed that teenagers who step away from social media apps for one to three weeks experience rapid improvements in emotional well-being. The boost in mood and reduction in anxiety matched the positive relief young people typically achieve through weeks of professional mental health counseling. (Stepping away from social media notifications for two weeks acted like a mental reset button, clearing away the constant pressure of comparing everyday life to polished highlights online.) Read the complete clinical review on After Babel.

Culture, Media & the Arts

Levi’s and Japanese Label Sacai Turn Classic Denim into High-Fashion Outerwear

Chitose Abe rebuilds everyday American trucker jackets with luxury sherpa lining and built-in belts.

American denim giant Levi’s teamed up with Japanese luxury streetwear brand Sacai to release a four-piece outerwear capsule. Sacai designer Chitose Abe rebuilt standard Levi's pieces from the ground up, adding warm sherpa linings, sleek leather trims, and integrated belt systems to denim jackets and flared jeans. While everyday 501 jeans sell for under $100, the high-fashion reimagining commands prices between $395 for belted trousers and $795 for heavy winter coats. (Think of regular blue jeans like a standard cotton t-shirt you wear to gym class. A high-fashion designer takes that plain shirt, cuts it into sharp angles, adds military-grade buckles, and turns it into a high-end runway statement piece.) Explore the complete collection details in InsideHook.

Actor Emma D'Arcy Shares an Obsession with Stone Carving and Mk.gee's Raw Guitar

The House of the Dragon star champions tactile craftsmanship, survival television, and messy teenage yearning.

Actor Emma D'Arcy sat down with culture newsletter Perfectly Imperfect to share personal cultural obsessions outside of Hollywood sets. D'Arcy praised indie musician Mk.gee's record Two Star & The Dream Police for channeling raw, nostalgic guitar energy, praised the wilderness reality show Alone for its gritty documentary style, and highlighted a lifelong fascination with historic stone carving tools and gargoyle masonry. Read the full recommendations list on Perfectly Imperfect.

Gaza Documentary Screening Draws Peaceful Crowds in the Hamptons

A sold-out premiere at the Sag Harbor Cinema brings passionate local audiences together without disruption.

Hundreds of filmgoers and local community members assembled outside the Sag Harbor Cinema on eastern Long Island for the sold-out premiere of NAZA, an acclaimed documentary directed by award-winning filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. Local authorities reported that the peaceful screening and sidewalk demonstrations concluded without incident. Read the local dispatch in Feed Me.

Tech Reporter Mike Isaac Leaves The New York Times for The Atlantic

A leading Silicon Valley investigative scoop-maker transitions to long-form magazine journalism.

Veteran technology correspondent Mike Isaac spent twelve years breaking front-page scoops about Uber, Meta, and startup boardroom battles for The New York Times. This week, Isaac announced a move to The Atlantic as a senior writer to spearhead deep investigative profiles across the tech landscape. Read about the newsroom move in Feed Me.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• YouTube Cracks Down on Automated "Clipping" Accounts on Shorts: YouTube introduced new guidelines that reward original videographers while demoting accounts that chop up popular livestreams into thousands of spammy short clips. Read the policy shift on creator algorithms in Garbage Day.

• Viral "AI Video Game Mashups" Turn Out to Be Screen-Recording Tricks: Viral clips claiming new artificial intelligence models magically combined Tony Hawk with Kingdom Hearts proved fake, relying on two games running side-by-side rather than real code rewrites. Follow the full technical breakdown in Feed Me.

• J.Crew Refreshes Rugged Workwear Sub-Brand Wallace & Barnes: Menswear brand J.Crew launched a fresh fall capsule for its long-running heritage line Wallace & Barnes, releasing heavy canvas chore jackets and thick flannel shirts. Check out the new autumn workwear catalog in InsideHook.

• Norway Considers Banning Smart Camera Glasses in Public Places: The Norwegian parliament will debate a temporary ban on Meta's video-recording smart glasses in public parks, beaches, schools, and locker rooms to protect citizen privacy. Check the policy report in 404 Media.

• Scientific Archive arXiv Slows Down Uploads to Fight AI Slop: The research paper hub arXiv announced strict daily submission caps after automated AI writing tools caused academic paper submissions to double over two years. Read the announcement in 404 Media.

• Frustrated Daters File Federal Complaints Against Match Group: Singles submitted formal complaints accusing Tinder and Hinge owner Match Group of manipulating matching algorithms to push lonely users toward $600 annual subscriptions. Review the regulatory report in 404 Media.

• The Wall Street Journal Recruits College Interns Two Years in Advance: The financial daily is already accepting student applications for summer 2027 internships in New York and London, showing how top media companies lock down talent earlier than ever. Find the job notice in Feed Me.

• Bennington College Launches Master's Program for Screenwriters: The Vermont liberal arts college created a graduate degree where students learn to write complete television pilot bibles and feature film scripts from scratch. Read the curriculum details in Feed Me.

• Newsletter Founder Tyler Denk Builds Giant Wellness Bathhouse: The founder of newsletter platform beehiiv opened a massive wellness bathhouse and sauna resort in Latin America as an unexpected hospitality side project. Check out the venue note in Feed Me.

• Brooklyn Shop Salter House Hosts Mary Shelley Literary Nights: A boutique in Brooklyn is gathering neighbors for live podcast recordings and community lectures about Mary Shelley's gothic novel Frankenstein. Explore the community calendar in Feed Me.

• Wall Street Hedge Funds Build $21 Million Private Office Clubs: Investment firms in Midtown Manhattan are spending millions constructing private restaurant floors, espresso bars, and gyms so traders gladly show up in person. Read the commercial real estate trend in Feed Me.

midday.body:
Monday, October 5, 2026

Today's Numbers

• $2.5 Billion: Nike plans to slash $2.5 billion in operational expenses and cut jobs as sneaker sales slow down across North America and China. (Feed Me)

• 45,000 Workers: Barclays ordered 45,000 UK bank employees back into physical offices three days a week, but postponed the deadline to 2027 for staff burdened by soaring train fares. (Feed Me)

• $100 Million: Modern artist Jeff Koons placed nine masterpieces from his private collection up for auction, including classic paintings by Picasso and Manet, to raise liquid cash. (Feed Me)

• $12 / Year: Vogue charges only $12 annually for a digital subscription, but fashion lovers expressed anger after parent publisher Condé Nast locked its decades-long runway show archive behind an expensive paywall. (Feed Me)

• $2 per Million Tokens: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol as an everyday developer model priced at $2 per million input tokens, offering an 80% price cut compared to flagship Astra models. (Lenny's Newsletter)

• 73 Cents: Total computing cost spent by software developer John Lindquist across 23 complete app development tests using Jev, proving that small AI decision engines make building custom software nearly free. (Lenny's Newsletter)

Quotes of the Day

"Our great hope with this is that he or one of his press people will call us horrible scumbags."

— Kurt Andersen, co-founder of satire magazine Spy, on reviving the publication for 30 days on Substack to reprint vintage investigative roasts of Donald Trump, via Feed Me

"Neighbors have taken to the water to protest him. Calling themselves 'kayak-tivists,' they form flotillas facing his island home, holding waterproof signs conveying their disappointment. A local newspaper columnist recommended that people in town give him the finger."

— The New York Times, reporting on Maine island locals paddling kayaks to protest Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts outside his vacation house, via Feed Me

"Getting to see it on my TV, in Taylor Swift’s hands, with Dakota’s reaction was really cool."

— Gabrielle Scelzo, New York baker behind backstage cakes at Saturday Night Live, on watching Taylor Swift present her custom cake to Dakota Johnson on live broadcast, via Feed Me

"The Face’s inability to get off the ground might just reflect the great divide between corporate publications like Vogue or independent Substacks that are not commercially tied to the industry so they’re able to deliver serious critique."

— Artemis Ward, design writer, explaining why legacy fashion magazines struggle to match the editorial freedom of independent newsletters, via Feed Me

"We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency."

— Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, discussing societal trade-offs in artificial intelligence development with Politico, via 404 Media

Artificial Intelligence & Digital Infrastructure

Meta Patches Dangerous "Escape" Bug in Its Muse AI Assistant Right Before Launch

Security engineers scrambled during a multi-team emergency to block users from jumping out of virtual sandboxes into private servers.

Meta engineers discovered serious security vulnerabilities in their viral AI agent "Muse" just weeks before its public rollout. At least one flaw could have allowed an ordinary user to break out of their assigned virtual machine and access Meta's sensitive internal databases. The discovery triggered emergency overtime work across infrastructure teams, reaching the desk of Mark Zuckerberg before engineers deployed a fix. (Think of an AI virtual machine like a locked hotel room: you can move the chairs around inside your room, but you should never be able to pick the lock and walk straight into the manager's master safe.) Read the full investigation in 404 Media.

OpenAI Product Teams Build "Disposable Software" with ChatGPT Sites

Fast development models allow engineers to create custom tools for a single business trip and discard them seven days later.

OpenAI product staff lead Kath Korevec demonstrated how internal teams use ChatGPT Sites to generate working dashboards connected to Slack, Notion, and team calendars in minutes. Instead of spending months coding permanent software, workers create narrow internal tools designed for single events or seven-day business trips, happily tossing them away when the project wraps up. (In the past, building a software tool felt like pouring concrete for a house—it took months and cost serious money. Today, building with AI feels like popping up a lightweight camping tent: you pitch it in five minutes, use it for the weekend, and pack it away when done.) Listen to the complete workflow walkthrough on Lenny's Newsletter.

Can the Government Kick Reporters Out of the White House and Censor AI Speech?

Legal scholars warn that upcoming court battles over autonomous agents will define First Amendment law for decades.

Speaking on Scott Galloway's podcast, free speech attorney Greg Lukianoff warned that political administrations are increasingly locking out journalists whose questions make them uncomfortable. More critically, Lukianoff highlighted an upcoming constitutional showdown: whether computer algorithms enjoy free speech rights. If federal regulators claim the power to dictate what opinions an AI model can generate, that authority could quickly expand to censor human digital speech. (Think of it like this: if you invent a robot that writes opinions, does that robot have freedom of speech like a newspaper writer, or can the mayor pull the plug whenever the machine criticizes city hall?) Hear the full legal debate on Prof G Media.

Law, Surveillance & Accountability

Oklahoma Federal Judge Strikes Down Routine Police Flock Camera Searches

A landmark court ruling declares that scanning out-of-state drivers without suspicion amounts to unconstitutional mass surveillance.

A federal judge in Oklahoma ruled that a police officer violated the U.S. Constitution by pulling over a driver based solely on automated license plate camera logs. The officer ran the car's plate through Flock Safety's camera database simply because it carried California plates, using past highway travel to justify searching the vehicle. The judge struck down the tactic as "indiscriminate mass surveillance" that directly violates Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable searches. (Imagine a police officer following you home from school every day just because your bicycle has a sticker from another city. The court ruled that police cannot treat every passing car as a criminal suspect without a specific, real reason.) Review the historic court ruling in 404 Media.

Youth, Cognition & Public Health

Jonathan Haidt Opens the Tech & Society Lab at NYU to Protect Young Minds

Researchers build open scientific tools to track how pocket screens and algorithms alter childhood development.

Social psychologist Jonathan Haidt and ten scientists at NYU Stern launched a dedicated laboratory to measure how smartphones and AI bots change developing brains. The lab studies how daily screen use disrupts classroom learning, sleep schedules, and face-to-face friendships, publishing practical research toolkits directly to schools, parents, and lawmakers. Explore their research findings at After Babel.

Taking a Two-Week Social Media Break Boosts Teen Mental Health Like Therapy

Clinical experiments show that stepping away from notifications delivers immediate drops in sadness and anxiety.

A major review of clinical experiments revealed that teenagers who step away from social media apps for one to three weeks experience rapid improvements in emotional well-being. The boost in mood and reduction in anxiety matched the positive relief young people typically achieve through weeks of professional mental health counseling. (Stepping away from social media notifications for two weeks acted like a mental reset button, clearing away the constant pressure of comparing everyday life to polished highlights online.) Read the complete clinical review on After Babel.

Culture, Media & the Arts

Actor Emma D'Arcy Shares an Obsession with Stone Carving and Mk.gee's Raw Guitar

The House of the Dragon star champions tactile craftsmanship, survival television, and messy teenage yearning.

Actor Emma D'Arcy sat down with culture newsletter Perfectly Imperfect to share personal cultural obsessions outside of Hollywood sets. D'Arcy praised indie musician Mk.gee's record Two Star & The Dream Police for channeling raw, nostalgic guitar energy, praised the wilderness reality show Alone for its gritty documentary style, and highlighted a lifelong fascination with historic stone carving tools and gargoyle masonry. Read the full recommendations list on Perfectly Imperfect.

Gaza Documentary Screening Draws Peaceful Crowds in the Hamptons

A sold-out premiere at the Sag Harbor Cinema brings passionate local audiences together without disruption.

Hundreds of filmgoers and local community members assembled outside the Sag Harbor Cinema on eastern Long Island for the sold-out premiere of NAZA, an acclaimed documentary directed by award-winning filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. Local authorities reported that the peaceful screening and sidewalk demonstrations concluded without incident. Read the local dispatch in Feed Me.

Tech Reporter Mike Isaac Leaves The New York Times for The Atlantic

A leading Silicon Valley investigative scoop-maker transitions to long-form magazine journalism.

Veteran technology correspondent Mike Isaac spent twelve years breaking front-page scoops about Uber, Meta, and startup boardroom battles for The New York Times. This week, Isaac announced a move to The Atlantic as a senior writer to spearhead deep investigative profiles across the tech landscape. Read about the newsroom move in Feed Me.

Quick Hits & Curiosities

• Norway Considers Banning Smart Camera Glasses in Public Places: The Norwegian parliament will debate a temporary ban on Meta's video-recording smart glasses in public parks, beaches, schools, and locker rooms to protect citizen privacy. Check the policy report in 404 Media.

• Scientific Archive arXiv Slows Down Uploads to Fight AI Slop: The research paper hub arXiv announced strict daily submission caps after automated AI writing tools caused academic paper submissions to double over two years. Read the announcement in 404 Media.

• Frustrated Daters File Federal Complaints Against Match Group: Singles submitted formal complaints accusing Tinder and Hinge owner Match Group of manipulating matching algorithms to push lonely users toward $600 annual subscriptions. Review the regulatory report in 404 Media.

• The Wall Street Journal Recruits College Interns Two Years in Advance: The financial daily is already accepting student applications for summer 2027 internships in New York and London, showing how top media companies lock down talent earlier than ever. Find the job notice in Feed Me.

• Bennington College Launches Master's Program for Screenwriters: The Vermont liberal arts college created a graduate degree where students learn to write complete television pilot bibles and feature film scripts from scratch. Read the curriculum details in Feed Me.

• Newsletter Founder Tyler Denk Builds Giant Wellness Bathhouse: The founder of newsletter platform beehiiv opened a massive wellness bathhouse and sauna resort in Latin America as an unexpected hospitality side project. Check out the venue note in Feed Me.

• Brooklyn Shop Salter House Hosts Mary Shelley Literary Nights: A boutique in Brooklyn is gathering neighbors for live podcast recordings and community lectures about Mary Shelley's gothic novel Frankenstein. Explore the community calendar in Feed Me.

• Wall Street Hedge Funds Build $21 Million Private Office Clubs: Investment firms in Midtown Manhattan are spending millions constructing private restaurant floors, espresso bars, and gyms so traders gladly show up in person. Read the commercial real estate trend in Feed Me.

• $2.5 Billion: Nike plans to slash $2.5 billion in operational expenses and cut jobs as sneaker sales slow down across North America and China. (Feed Me)

• $100 Million: Modern artist Jeff Koons placed nine masterpieces from his private collection up for auction, including classic paintings by Picasso and Manet, to raise liquid cash. (Feed Me)

• $12 / Year: Vogue charges only $12 annually for a digital subscription, but fashion lovers expressed anger after parent publisher Condé Nast locked its decades-long runway show archive behind an expensive paywall. (Feed Me)

• $2 per Million Tokens: OpenAI introduced GPT-6.1 Sol as an everyday developer model priced at $2 per million input tokens, offering an 80% price cut compared to flagship Astra models. (Lenny's Newsletter)

• 73 Cents: Total computing cost spent by software developer John Lindquist across 23 complete app development tests using Jev, proving that small AI decision engines make building custom software nearly free. (Lenny's Newsletter)

• 1,009 Drafts: Number of Wikipedia article submissions researchers audited to show how strictly the online encyclopedia rejects corporate pages. (Wikify)

• 6 Hours: Total slow-cooker cooking time for a velvety autumn butternut squash and apple soup topped with mango chutney and crunchy pumpkin seeds. (The New York Times)

Quotes of the Day

"Our great hope with this is that he or one of his press people will call us horrible scumbags."

— Kurt Andersen, co-founder of satire magazine Spy, on reviving the publication for 30 days on Substack to reprint vintage investigative roasts of Donald Trump, via Feed Me

"Neighbors have taken to the water to protest him. Calling themselves 'kayak-tivists,' they form flotillas facing his island home, holding waterproof signs conveying their disappointment. A local newspaper columnist recommended that people in town give him the finger."

— The New York Times, reporting on Maine island locals paddling kayaks to protest Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts outside his vacation house, via Feed Me

"Getting to see it on my TV, in Taylor Swift’s hands, with Dakota’s reaction was really cool."

— Gabrielle Scelzo, New York baker behind backstage cakes at Saturday Night Live, on watching Taylor Swift present her custom cake to Dakota Johnson on live broadcast, via Feed Me

"The Face’s inability to get off the ground might just reflect the great divide between corporate publications like Vogue or independent Substacks that are not commercially tied to the industry so they’re able to deliver serious critique."

— Artemis Ward, design writer, explaining why legacy fashion magazines struggle to match the editorial freedom of independent newsletters, via Feed Me

"We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency."

— Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, discussing societal trade-offs in artificial intelligence development with Politico, via 404 Media

"In general, my intrigue with any sort of style-forward apparel was largely predicated on what looked good with Nike or Adidas footwear... I was much more enamored with Jordans and Yeezys than anything Kris Van Assche was doing at Dior."

— Paolo Sandoval, editor of The Goods, on how 2010s sneaker forums launched a generation of menswear obsession, via InsideHook

Artificial Intelligence & Digital Infrastructure

Meta Patches Dangerous "Escape" Bug in Its Muse AI Assistant Right Before Launch

Security engineers scrambled during a multi-team emergency to block users from jumping out of virtual sandboxes into private servers.

Meta engineers discovered serious security vulnerabilities in their viral AI agent "Muse" just weeks before its public rollout. At least one flaw could have allowed an ordinary user to break out of their assigned virtual machine and access Meta's sensitive internal databases. The discovery triggered emergency overtime work across infrastructure teams, reaching the desk of Mark Zuckerberg before engineers deployed a fix. (Think of an AI virtual machine like a locked hotel room: you can move the chairs around inside your room, but you should never be able to pick the lock and walk straight into the manager's master safe.) Read the full investigation in 404 Media.

OpenAI Product Teams Build "Disposable Software" with ChatGPT Sites

Fast development models allow engineers to create custom tools for a single business trip and discard them seven days later.

OpenAI product staff lead Kath Korevec demonstrated how internal teams use ChatGPT Sites to generate working dashboards connected to Slack, Notion, and team calendars in minutes. Instead of spending months coding permanent software, workers create narrow internal tools designed for single events or seven-day business trips, happily tossing them away when the project wraps up. (In the past, building a software tool felt like pouring concrete for a house—it took months and cost serious money. Today, building with AI feels like popping up a lightweight camping tent: you pitch it in five minutes, use it for the weekend, and pack it away when done.) Listen to the complete workflow walkthrough on Lenny's Newsletter.

Can the Government Kick Reporters Out of the White House and Censor AI Speech?

Legal scholars warn that upcoming court battles over autonomous agents will define First Amendment law for decades.

Speaking on Scott Galloway's podcast, free speech attorney Greg Lukianoff warned that political administrations are increasingly locking out journalists whose questions make them uncomfortable. More critically, Lukianoff highlighted an upcoming constitutional showdown: whether computer algorithms enjoy free speech rights. If federal regulators claim the power to dictate what opinions an AI model can generate, that authority could quickly expand to censor human digital speech. (Think of it like this: if you invent a robot that writes opinions, does that robot have freedom of speech like a newspaper writer, or can the mayor pull the plug whenever the machine criticizes city hall?) Hear the full legal debate on Prof G Media.

Law, Surveillance & Accountability

Oklahoma Federal Judge Strikes Down Routine Police Flock Camera Searches

A landmark court ruling declares that scanning out-of-state drivers without suspicion amounts to unconstitutional mass surveillance.

A federal judge in Oklahoma ruled that a police officer violated the U.S. Constitution by pulling over a driver based solely on automated license plate camera logs. The officer ran the car's plate through Flock Safety's camera database simply because it carried California plates, using past highway travel to justify searching the vehicle. The judge struck down the tactic as "indiscriminate mass surveillance" that directly violates Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable searches. (Imagine a police officer following you home from school every day just because your bicycle has a sticker from another city. The court ruled that police cannot treat every passing car as a criminal suspect without a specific, real reason.) Review the historic court ruling in 404 Media.

Youth, Cognition & Public Health

Jonathan Haidt Opens the Tech & Society Lab at NYU to Protect Young Minds

Researchers build open scientific tools to track how pocket screens and algorithms alter childhood development.

Social psychologist Jonathan Haidt and ten scientists at NYU Stern launched a dedicated laboratory to measure how smartphones and AI bots change developing brains. The lab studies how daily screen use disrupts classroom learning, sleep schedules, and face-to-face friendships, publishing practical research toolkits directly to schools, parents, and lawmakers. Explore their research findings at After Babel.

Taking a Two-Week Social Media Break Boosts Teen Mental Health Like Therapy

Clinical experiments show that stepping away from notifications delivers immediate drops in sadness and anxiety.

Global Politics & Internet Culture

Brazil’s Online Culture Wars Reveal How Social Apps Protect Right-Wing Leaders

Evangelical social channels and online loan apps help far-right politicians keep power even after losing national elections.

Brazil's right-wing political movement scored huge legislative wins this weekend, forcing current President Lula da Silva into a tough runoff election against former leader Jair Bolsonaro’s son Flavio. Internet researcher Ryan Broderick reported that right-wing candidates stayed wildly popular through massive online communities rather than traditional news. Popular church leaders like Bruno Leonardo—whose YouTube channel commands nearly 80 million subscribers—rack up millions of daily views by asking followers to comment prayers. Meanwhile, easy phone-based loan services left over 80% of Brazilian households in debt, creating economic anxiety that right-wing media channels exploit. (Think of social media algorithms like a giant megaphone that gives the loudest voices free extra batteries. Even if voters elect a new leader, the megaphone keeps replaying the old leader's songs, keeping their political movement alive online forever.) Read the deep-dive report on international digital politics in Garbage Day.

A major review of clinical experiments revealed that teenagers who step away from social media apps for one to three weeks experience rapid improvements in emotional well-being. The boost in mood and reduction in anxiety matched the positive relief young people typically achieve through weeks of professional mental health counseling. (Stepping away from social media notifications for two weeks acted like a mental reset button, clearing away the constant pressure of comparing everyday life to polished highlights online.) Read the complete clinical review on After Babel.

Chitose Abe rebuilds everyday American trucker jackets with luxury sherpa lining and built-in belts.

American denim giant Levi’s teamed up with Japanese luxury streetwear brand Sacai to release a four-piece outerwear capsule. Sacai designer Chitose Abe rebuilt standard Levi's pieces from the ground up, adding warm sherpa linings, sleek leather trims, and integrated belt systems to denim jackets and flared jeans. While everyday 501 jeans sell for under $100, the high-fashion reimagining commands prices between $395 for belted trousers and $795 for heavy winter coats. (Think of regular blue jeans like a standard cotton t-shirt you wear to gym class. A high-fashion designer takes that plain shirt, cuts it into sharp angles, adds military-grade buckles, and turns it into a high-end runway statement piece.) Explore the complete collection details in InsideHook.

The House of the Dragon star champions tactile craftsmanship, survival television, and messy teenage yearning.

Actor Emma D'Arcy sat down with culture newsletter Perfectly Imperfect to share personal cultural obsessions outside of Hollywood sets. D'Arcy praised indie musician Mk.gee's record Two Star & The Dream Police for channeling raw, nostalgic guitar energy, praised the wilderness reality show Alone for its gritty documentary style, and highlighted a lifelong fascination with historic stone carving tools and gargoyle masonry. Read the full recommendations list on Perfectly Imperfect.

A sold-out premiere at the Sag Harbor Cinema brings passionate local audiences together without disruption.

Hundreds of filmgoers and local community members assembled outside the Sag Harbor Cinema on eastern Long Island for the sold-out premiere of NAZA, an acclaimed documentary directed by award-winning filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. Local authorities reported that the peaceful screening and sidewalk demonstrations concluded without incident. Read the local dispatch in Feed Me.

OpenAI product staff lead Kath Korevec demonstrated how internal teams use ChatGPT Sites to generate working dashboards connected to Slack, Notion, and team calendars in minutes. Instead of spending months coding permanent software, workers create narrow internal tools designed for single events or seven-day business trips, happily tossing them away when the project wraps up. (In the past, building a software tool felt like pouring concrete for a house—it took months and cost serious money. Today, building with AI feels like popping up a lightweight camping tent: you pitch it in five minutes, use it for the weekend, and pack it away when done.) Listen to the complete workflow walkthrough on Lenny's Newsletter.

Can the Government Kick Reporters Out of the White House and Censor AI Speech?

Legal scholars warn that upcoming court battles over autonomous agents will define First Amendment law for decades.

Speaking on Scott Galloway's podcast, free speech attorney Greg Lukianoff warned that political administrations are increasingly locking out journalists whose questions make them uncomfortable. More critically, Lukianoff highlighted an upcoming constitutional showdown: whether computer algorithms enjoy free speech rights. If federal regulators claim the power to dictate what opinions an AI model can generate, that authority could quickly expand to censor human digital speech. (Think of it like this: if you invent a robot that writes opinions, does that robot have freedom of speech like a newspaper writer, or can the mayor pull the plug whenever the machine criticizes city hall?) Hear the full legal debate on Prof G Media.

Law, Surveillance & Accountability

Oklahoma Federal Judge Strikes Down Routine Police Flock Camera Searches

A landmark court ruling declares that scanning out-of-state drivers without suspicion amounts to unconstitutional mass surveillance.

A federal judge in Oklahoma ruled that a police officer violated the U.S. Constitution by pulling over a driver based solely on automated license plate camera logs. The officer ran the car's plate through Flock Safety's camera database simply because it carried California plates, using past highway travel to justify searching the vehicle. The judge struck down the tactic as "indiscriminate mass surveillance" that directly violates Fourth Amendment protections against unreasonable searches. (Imagine a police officer following you home from school every day just because your bicycle has a sticker from another city. The court ruled that police cannot treat every passing car as a criminal suspect without a specific, real reason.) Review the historic court ruling in 404 Media.

Social psychologist Jonathan Haidt and ten scientists at NYU Stern launched a dedicated laboratory to measure how smartphones and AI bots change developing brains. Global Politics & Internet Culture

Brazil’s Online Culture Wars Reveal How Social Apps Protect Right-Wing Leaders

Evangelical social channels and online loan apps help far-right politicians keep power even after losing national elections.

Brazil's right-wing political movement scored huge legislative wins this weekend, forcing current President Lula da Silva into a tough runoff election against former leader Jair Bolsonaro’s son Flavio. Internet researcher Ryan Broderick reported that right-wing candidates stayed wildly popular through massive online communities rather than traditional news. Popular church leaders like Bruno Leonardo—whose YouTube channel commands nearly 80 million subscribers—rack up millions of daily views by asking followers to comment prayers. Meanwhile, easy phone-based loan services left over 80% of Brazilian households in debt, creating economic anxiety that right-wing media channels exploit. (Think of social media algorithms like a giant megaphone that gives the loudest voices free extra batteries. Even if voters elect a new leader, the megaphone keeps replaying the old leader's songs, keeping their political movement alive online forever.) Read the deep-dive report on international digital politics in Garbage Day.

A major review of clinical experiments revealed that teenagers who step away from social media apps for one to three weeks experience rapid improvements in emotional well-being. The boost in mood and reduction in anxiety matched the positive relief young people typically achieve through weeks of professional mental health counseling. (Stepping away from social media notifications for two weeks acted like a mental reset button, clearing away the constant pressure of comparing everyday life to polished highlights online.) Read the complete clinical review on After Babel.
